Welcome to the Victoria II military tutorial. You are ruling Belgium, a small nation with great potential. However, there is a problem: your Dutch neighbor has just declared war on you.

The Dutch are massing on our border, we must drive them away. The first thing we need to do is select an army to do this. Click on the army in Brussels to select an army, which has been circled on the map.

The army you just selected, the First Infantry Division, consists of 12,000 men from four brigades. In the unit interface you can see each brigade and its headcount. In the unit interface you can also find the following data:
Number of soldiers and brigades. If engaged in combat, the number of soldiers will decrease. However, if there are unemployed soldiers in your nation, these units will replenish automatically.
The general of your army. His traits will affect the army's performance

Manpower and organization. The green (left) bar is organization, which represents your unit's willingness to fight. The higher this value, the more efficient your troops are in combat. Organization is lost in combat but recovers on its own. The yellow (right) bar represents manpower. When this bar is full, your unit has maximum manpower. If it's not full, the unit has suffered losses that have not been replenished.

The supply status of your unit. Every unit needs certain things to maintain operation, and these will be automatically extracted from your stockpile. If you cannot provide these things, it will damage the speed of manpower replenishment and organization recovery.
Take some time to hover over the icons in the unit interface for more information
To occupy the Netherlands we need to send more troops to the border. However, we cannot leave the capital undefended, so we must split our forces.

A new unit has been established, and now you can see the army organization interface. To add units to this force, click the move button to move the sub-units you want to split. Try moving a unit to the new force.
Please click the split army icon
Well done, there should be two units in Brussels now. You may also notice the small flag next to the Belgian flag flying by your army. This indicates there is more than one unit here.

However, the Dutch might easily defeat this force, so we should merge them again. First, use a drag box to select both units in this province. If you selected other units outside the province, press ESC on your keyboard and try again.
After selecting units, press the merge units button.

Now we must march toward the evil Dutch. We want to move the force in Brussels to deal with the Dutch army in Maastricht. Select the force in Brussels and then right-click Maastricht to move your force.
Notice the arrow pointing from your unit to Maastricht. As your unit advances, this arrow will gradually fill up, indicating how far your force has marched. Press the spacebar to unpause.
Your unit is now moving. Notice how the arrow fills up.

Your unit is acting against the Dutch. Notice the progress bar below your force, which shows who is at an advantage. More yellow indicates the side with the flag on the left is at an advantage, more green indicates the nation on the right is at an advantage. Click on the progress bar for more battle details.
The battle interface should have appeared. Here you can get more detailed information about what's happening in the battle. Press the spacebar again to unpause. We'll soon win.
The battle is over, and your force should have won. In the battle result window, you can see the results of this action. Click Next to continue.
Clicking on the map is not the only way to select units. Victoria II has a feature called the shortcut bar. Click the small plus sign on the right to open the shortcut bar window.
The shortcut bar is a shortcut for managing many things in your nation, such as your army, battles, and ongoing construction. You can toggle the small icons on the shortcut bar to customize it.
Now we want to select the Third Infantry Division, so click on this unit in the shortcut bar.
To raid the Dutch, we will land behind their lines. Make sure you have selected the force in Brussels. Note you have a fleet in the port of Bruges (a ship by the dock).
Load your units onto ships by clicking the load button on the right.

Now we must move our units to the sea area "Dogger Bank." To do this, click the port of Bruges, and after the fleet is selected, right-click "Dogger Bank" and continue the game after your movement arrow appears.

Now we must land. Make sure you have selected your navy. Note the button in the lower right corner of the unit interface, click this to select your units. Click this and right-click Middelburg to move your units there.
Welcome to the tutorial on the industry part of Victoria II. Here we will learn about the most fundamental part of building your nation in Victoria II: the economy.
The economy is built around money and goods. Goods are produced and consumed by your people and troops, while money is used to pass goods from producers to consumers.
Click the production button in the top toolbar to get an overview of the production of goods in your nation.

One of the most fundamental driving forces in Victoria II is the circulation of goods, which can range from timber to light weapons. Goods are produced by producers and purchased by consumers. Consumers can be people looking for something to eat or producers in need of raw materials.
Most of this circulation takes place without your involvement. Your interaction with this process can be building factories, taxing trade, and purchasing goods to supply your army.
There are three sources of goods production:
RGOs - These are farms and mines. Farmers and laborers accept nature's bounty here.
Artisans - These are blacksmith shops and textile workshops. They purchase products from the market and produce processed goods.

Factories - Factories also produce processed goods. However, these are the path of future development. Depending on the political system, they may be built by the player or by capitalists. Factories employ workers and clerks for production.
In this interface you can see all goods produced by your nation. They are grouped by category, and next to each produced good there is an icon indicating which type of producer made it.
Artisans represent the part they produce themselves
In this interface you can hover over various icons for more information about domestic production to help you make decisions

Your nation is Belgium, and you must manage its national finances to achieve leadership in the world. Taxes must be balanced with spending, and funds must be saved for investments such as the military. We must open the finance interface to manage finances. Click the finance button in the top toolbar.
Here is the finance interface. Here you can manage your government's income and expenses, and also take loans to quickly increase cash. Let's start with taxes. Click Next to continue
Your most important way to generate income is taxation. Tax rates can be set differently for different social classes.
Different occupations belong to different classes. You can tell which ones by looking at the icons next to the tax sliders.

Taxes are set by moving the sliders for each class. However, taxation has consequences. The more tax you collect, the less money you leave to your people. Next to the tax slider you can see a chart showing the satisfaction level this class needs. Try to keep taxes as low as possible while maintaining a balanced budget. Click Next to continue.

So what can we do with the taxes we collect? First we use it to maintain the government. There are many items of expenditure, such as military spending, education spending, and funds to maintain your army and colonies.

There are two types of spending. The first is fixed spending, which depends on the products you purchase, such as military maintenance. These expenditures change based on your actions in other parts of the game, such as disbanding a unit.
The second type can be adjusted via sliders. The more you move to the right, the more funds you pay.

Most of the time you must prioritize your spending. Need more troops? Increase military spending. Want to expand the bureaucracy? Move the administrative spending slider. Try moving the slider and see how the numbers change. Note that all changes are gradual — if you increase the administrative spending slider, more people will want to become bureaucrats over time. When you're done, click Next.

Belgium needs a balanced budget. You achieve this by making income equal to expenses. However, every slider you move has its pros and cons — higher taxes will consume your people's assets, and lower spending will damage your government's finances.
If your finances are not balanced and available funds run out, we will automatically take a loan. Now, let's try balancing your budget. When you think it's ready, click Next.
When your economy needs a short-term boost, you can always borrow money. This money comes from people depositing surplus funds in the national bank.
When you take a loan, the money is first borrowed from your own people, then from people of other nations.
Try getting a loan by clicking the take loan button. Push the slider to the amount you want, then click Next.

You now have a loan, and you can see your total borrowing has increased by the amount you just applied for. Also note the interest rate — this is the interest your loan requires per day. However, interest is expensive, so we must repay our loan now. Click repay loan and push the slider all the way to the right before clicking "OK."
To advance in the world you need research. Research can enhance everything from your military to your industry. To manage research, open the research interface.

This is the research interface, where you can start researching your technologies. Technologies are divided into five categories: Army, Navy, Commerce, Culture, and Industry. Belgium is a developing industrial nation, so let's click Industry.
Now all the industrial technologies are displayed before you. Green ones you already have. Yellow ones you can research. Gray ones you cannot research yet.
In the process of becoming an industrial nation, we must try to strengthen our infrastructure. Click Experimental Railways.
Notice the area in the lower right corner has changed. Here you can see the effect after the technology is completed and possible inventions. Click Start Research to begin this project.
Now the selected technology should turn blue. This means the project is underway. You can always change projects by researching another technology.

This tutorial will cover the political part of Victoria II. Politics is a more important part in Victoria II. As the game progresses, society will change, and new political ideas will take root among your people and begin to demand reforms.

Political parties and reforms have a significant impact on how you control your nation. How you manage your people depends on your will. To learn more about politics, click Politics in the top toolbar.

In this interface you can see the current ruling party. The tendencies and topics of your people and voters. If your government type allows, you can change the ruling party, or if you prefer democracy, you can start an election. Click Next to continue.

Here you can see your ruling party. A ruling party has an ideology and a set of policies. These policies affect how your nation runs — for example, whether the state can build factories or only capitalists can. They also restrict the use of sliders in the finance interface.

Belgium is ruled by the National Party. You can hover over the chart to learn more about their policies. As the game progresses, your needs will change, and so will your people's ideology and the policies they support. You must balance between the type of government you want and what your people want. When you're ready, click Next.
To influence how your nation runs, you can implement a series of social and political reforms.
Political reforms affect your nation's political system, while social reforms use government funds to help different groups of people.

You should consider signing the reforms your people expect, and you must be careful to ensure you can afford them. The upper house must also be considered — they debate whether new reforms should be implemented. Here are some examples of Belgian reforms:

Electoral System — Belgium has a wealth-based voting system. This means only the rich and middle classes can vote. If you change it to universal suffrage weighted, all groups can vote, but the wealthy get double votes.

Healthcare — Belgium has "symbolic healthcare." This means with a certain investment, our population growth will increase by an additional 2.5%. But only if we have sufficient investment in our finances.

Here you can see how your people feel about your nation. Note the two charts: Voter Ideology and Popular Ideology. The reason for this difference is our voting system, which is also a political reform.
One effect of this difference is that when a party wins an election, most of our people may feel uneasy about it.
Below you can see the policies most important to our people. This may be an important consideration when implementing reforms.
Your population is your most important resource and the most important driving force in Victoria II. Your population produces goods, purchases goods, pays taxes, votes, or rebels when unhappy.
The population interface is your main source of population information. But first, let's talk about where your people live: provinces and regions.
Click on the province of Brussels in the middle of your map.

The large map is divided into many provinces, which are the smallest geographic units. Your population lives and works within these. Provinces are divided into several regions. Each region typically contains one to four provinces.
Each province shares certain things with its region, such as factories producing goods, bureaucrats responsible for tax collection, and capitalists and nobles who employ workers.

At the top of the province interface you selected is the name of the region this province belongs to: "Flanders," and below that is the province's name. In Victoria II there are many indirect ways to influence your population, but there is also a more direct way to influence the population of this province: the national focus.
To set a national focus, click the national focus button on the province interface.
Compared to other means, national focus is the most direct and effective way to influence the local population.
Railways — Encourage capitalists to build railways
Migration — Encourage your population to move here
Colonization — Establish a colony in this region, only usable in empty regions
Assimilation — Encourage your population to assimilate into a certain group
Production — Encourage your capitalists and artisans to produce a certain type of goods
To increase Belgium's industrial output we need more workers, click the craftsman icon to achieve this goal.
In the province interface you can also view the population situation of that province. The three icons from left to right represent their occupation, ideology, and ethnicity.
Also, click the View button next to the chart to see more information. Try it now.

This is your population interface, where you can view the population situation across Belgium. Click Brussels to see detailed information about the people of Brussels. By selecting different provinces, regions, or the entire nation, you can view the population situation across different scopes.
The filter keys at the top allow you to select different occupations to get the information you want.
This is the statistical status of your currently selected population, such as their occupation, ethnicity, and religion.

Here is a long list of the province's population divided by occupation, ethnicity, and religion, called Pops. Want to know about each pop? Find and click the Flemish Craftsman icon in the list on the left.

Pops are the smallest population unit divided by ethnicity, religion, and occupation. In this interface you can see their satisfaction. You can also view their attitude toward politics here. Click Next to continue.

In Victoria II, goods are produced from various sources such as RGOs, factories, and artisans. These goods are then sold for money, and most of these transactions happen automatically between the people and factories. Some are controlled by the player, such as purchasing goods to build and supply the army, build factories, and support overseas territories. These are controlled in the trade interface. Click the Trade button in the top toolbar.

Here is the trade interface, where you can find much information about the flow of goods in the market. In the upper left corner of the interface, you can see all goods in the game, along with their prices and latest price changes. We need some information about light weapons, click the light weapons icon.
Notice the area in the upper right corner has changed, now showing the details of this good.
At the top you can see a price chart showing how prices change over time.

Below there are two checkboxes: Auto and Domestic Purchase. Selecting Auto will automatically purchase the goods your army needs. Domestic Purchase will force you to only buy goods produced domestically.
Here you can also see how much your nation produces and the needs of the government, producers, and people. Now we need to buy some things. Click Next to continue.
The Dutch seem like a threat, we must stockpile some cannons for the future, cannons are necessary for building and supplying the army.
Notice the icon with "buy" text and the slider next to it below. This means if you move the slider to a value in your stockpile, the game will try to buy until you have this quantity.

On the other hand, if you click this icon again, it will change to sell, and you will sell your stockpile until the value you set. Now we want to buy, so make sure the buy/sell button is set to buy and confirm your order by clicking the confirm trade button after moving the slider to about 10 units.

Now turn your attention to the national stockpile. Here you can see how much goods your government has stored and their changes from the previous day. Also note this button — clicking it will allow your people to purchase goods from your stockpile, which is very useful when you cannot buy from abroad during wartime, if you have prepared and stockpiled strategic goods.
Now continue the game for a few days to see how the stockpile gets filled with light weapons.

Diplomacy is the most important tool for dominating the world in Victoria II. Here you form alliances and declare war. You pull small nations into your sphere of influence and monitor your status among the Great Powers. Click the Diplomacy button in the top toolbar.
This is the diplomacy interface. Here you control your nation's diplomatic decisions and observe other nations.

The first thing you need to do is take action against our northern enemy. However, the Netherlands is somewhat stronger than us, so we need allies. Britain is a good candidate — find Britain in the country list in the lower left corner. Try using the filter button on the list to help you find Britain.

Now we have selected Britain. Before we ally with them, we first need to know if they like us. Look at the right side of the list you just clicked. This value is still relatively low but should be enough. Now let's check if they are involved in other conflicts. Click the Show Wars button at the top of the interface.

Now all ongoing wars should be visible at the top of the interface. You should be able to see the Texans fighting their former Mexican rulers. You can also view Britain's allies and war status in the middle-right.

To ally with Britain we need to start with diplomacy. Diplomacy includes various options from allying to declaring war. To execute diplomatic commands we need diplomatic points, which increase each month. In the diplomacy bar above we can see we have 1 diplomatic point, just enough to ally with Britain. Go to the diplomacy interface and click Alliance with 'Accept' to suggest Britain ally with us.

Now Britain is our ally. Generally we need to wait a few days to get a response from other nations, but this time it was quick. Now it's time to deal with the Dutch. Click the Netherlands in the diplomacy interface and click the Declare War button.

To declare war you need a war goal, and the war goals we can choose from are limited at declaration. If the war goes well we can add more goals, but if we fail to achieve these goals our people will be very angry. For now we just need to humiliate the Dutch, and if we win we can reduce their prestige. Continue by clicking the Humiliate button.

Declaring war has a cost — it affects how other nations see us. There is a value called infamy. If infamy is too high we will have a lot of trouble, such as other nations forming righteous alliances to sanction our nation.
War also has rewards. After completing war goals we can also gain some prestige, and the prestige reward varies depending on the war goal.
Each war goal also requires a certain amount of war score to achieve. The higher the war score, the easier it is for the enemy to accept our demands.
Now everything is ready, just click the "Agree" button to declare war on the other side.

In this chapter, we will introduce concepts of the military system familiar to veteran Victoria players but new to beginners. Please click the military button at the top to enter the military interface.
This is the military panel, where you can view your army and generals, recruit troops and mobilize the nation for war. Please click the Raise Army button to start recruiting troops.

In Victoria, the concept of manpower differs from other Paradox games. All armies are recruited from the population with the occupation of soldiers, the soldier pop. The prerequisite for building an army is having enough soldiers in the population to fill it. The list shows all units that can be recruited now. If you need to recruit more units, increase the military budget to encourage more people to join the military. Please click Walloon Infantry.

The unit we just clicked is called "Walloon Infantry." This means it is a regular infantry unit composed of Walloon soldiers. Below the unit name it says Brussels, indicating that the soldiers of this unit live in Brussels.

The icon and number on the left of the unit represent the materials needed to build the army. This unit needs 20 light weapons and 20 canned food. These materials come from your stockpile. If stock is insufficient, you need to purchase from the global market.

The unit being built is displayed in the build queue on the right side of the screen, and you can click it to cancel the build command. Please click the Close button to continue to the next part of the tutorial.
To achieve victory, the army must have correct leadership from generals. Recruiting army generals and navy generals consumes leadership.

Leadership comes from the population with the occupation of officers, the officer pop. If you need to recruit more generals, increase the military budget in the budget panel (same as increasing soldiers). The difference between officers and soldiers is that soldiers are recruited from the poor population, while officers are recruited from the rich population.
The number next to the recruit general button indicates how many generals can be recruited with current leadership. Please click the Promote Army General button.
This general has two traits, which can be beneficial or harmful. Hover over traits to see details. Whether traits are good or bad, an army with a general is always stronger than one without.
View the troops the general is leading — this new general is not currently assigned to command any troops.
Click the box to select automatic assignment of generals to command troops and automatic recruitment of generals.
Now manually assign generals to command troops. Please select the unit in Spa according to the arrow direction.
Click the "(No Commander)" box, then select a general.

In this chapter, we will introduce production concepts of the Victoria series familiar to veteran players. First, the most basic goods producers: RGOs. Please click the province of Brussels to open the province panel.
Many goods are produced by RGOs. RGOs essentially refer to farms and mines. In the province panel you can see the RGOs of Brussels: sulfur mines.
Products - The icon shows that this RGO produces sulfur, and the number next to it shows the quantity produced. Hover over the product to see factors affecting productivity.
Income - All RGO products will flow into the market. RGOs earn income after successfully selling their goods. Income is used to pay workers and the nobles who own these RGOs.
Employees - RGOs hire farmers and laborers to work in farms and mines. More employees bring more products, but the maximum number of employees is limited.

You cannot directly affect RGO output. But you can make them more efficient and feel more attractive to work in by researching technology, building railways, and tax reform. Hover over each small icon to see more information. When done, click the production button at the top.
This panel shows factories built in various provinces.
Raw Materials - Factories need raw materials purchased from the world market to manufacture products.
Maintenance - In addition to raw materials, factories need cement for maintenance. Lack of cement will cause reduced output.

When there aren't enough resources, you can prioritize a factory. Here iron is needed by several factories, please click the box as indicated by the button to give the steel mill priority over iron resources.
In this panel you can see factories that can be built.

Click the General Clothing Factory in the menu to see which raw materials needed by this factory can be produced domestically. Belgium already has textile factories. Building more factories using textiles as raw materials can strengthen the local economy.

Below you can see the construction materials needed to build the factory. When clicking the build button, insufficient raw materials will be automatically purchased from the world market. In addition, the raw material cost is listed below. Raw material cost refers to the funds used to purchase factory raw materials in the first few days of factory operation.
This column shows the number of unemployed workers. In the absence of unemployed workers, new factories will gradually employ workers transferred from other occupations.

The criteria for selecting factories should be to build factories whose raw materials can be produced locally and for whose products there is demand. Now click Start Building to build the General Clothing Factory.

Factory output can be increased by expanding the factory. Whether factories are expanded by the player or by capitalists also depends on the political system. The cost of expanding a factory is similar to building a similar new factory. You can hover over the expand button to see the expansion cost.
Please click the Expand button to expand the steel mill.

Factory products flow into the global market. Sales revenue depends on current prices and sales volume. A portion of sales revenue is used to purchase raw materials, and the remainder is profit. Profit is paid to workers (craftsmen and clerks) and owners (capitalists). The player does not directly receive profit money, but only indirectly through taxes and tariffs. Please ensure factory profitability — unprofitable factories will lay off workers and cause unemployment. Click Next to continue.
In this chapter, we will introduce finance concepts unique to Victoria II that differ from other Paradox games. First, please open the finance interface.
In Victoria II, taxation depends on population income. Whenever a population earns an income, you receive a portion of it through taxes. Populations are divided into three classes:
Middle class - Including artisans, clergy, and other educated populations.
Rich class - Including nobles and capitalists.

The chart next to each class shows their standard of living. For example, whether they have enough life necessities. If you see too much red, you can help improve their lives by lowering taxes. Hover over specific population icons to see the living conditions of people in different occupations. Click Next to continue the tutorial.

Tariffs refer to taxes or subsidies on international trade. Pulling the tariff bar to the right increases the burden on the population and factories when purchasing foreign goods. Pulling to the left means the state subsidizes their purchases.
Tariffs can serve the dual purpose of increasing revenue and protecting domestic industry.
Industrial Subsidies - This expenditure subsidizes unprofitable factories. Can be activated in the production interface.

Stockpile Expenditure - Used to pay for daily trade costs set in the trade interface. There are two numbers above the slider: military consumption and overseas maintenance costs. These numbers indirectly affect storage expenditure, because maintaining troops and assets requires purchasing materials. For example, after building factories and recruiting armies or navies that need supplies, you need to purchase maintenance goods through auto-trade or manual trade.

Education Expenditure - Used to pay clergy salaries. Clergy have the role of educating the population and reducing population consciousness. The higher the expenditure, the more people want to become clergy.

Administrative Expenditure - Used to pay bureaucrat salaries. Bureaucrats are responsible for running social reforms and collecting taxes. More bureaucrats make tax collection more efficient. National administrative efficiency is shown above the administrative expenditure slider.
Social Expenditure - Used to pay for various social reforms, such as unemployment benefits and pensions.
Military Expenditure - Used to pay soldier and officer salaries.

All these expenditures are directly paid to various types of citizens. If you pay too little, these people will start looking for new jobs. If you pay a lot, you can attract people from other occupations, of course this also increases expenditure. Please decide the best expenditure so that the number of people working in various industries is what you need. Click Next to continue.

Diplomacy can also generate income or expenditure. Such as war subsidies — we may need to spend money to support friendly nations, or we may receive support from friendly nations. War reparations can also bring income. Click Next to continue.
In this chapter, we will further familiarize ourselves with the impact of research on the nation. Please click the research button at the top to enter the research interface.

Each technology research has "research points." These refer to the research points that must be accumulated to complete the technology. Click any technology to see the research points required for it in the info panel. Click Next.

Research points are generated by the population, specifically by clergy and bureaucrats. Literacy rate, national diversity, and technological progress all affect the generation of research points. Hover over the technology button at the top to see how many research points Belgium has. Now let's discuss the impact of technology, click the Strategic Mobility technology in the Army category.

Technology R&D has dual effects: immediate effects and inventions. The info panel explains that Strategic Mobility affects the maximum level of fortifications, army scouting, and supply consumption. These effects take effect immediately when the technology is successfully researched.

Inventions - Note the lightbulb next to the technology, these represent inventions. Hover over them to see their effects. Invention effects are not immediate, but are randomly triggered with a certain probability after the technology is completed. Gray lightbulbs indicate they cannot be triggered, yellow means possible, and green means already triggered.
The player can research what kind of inventions correspond to what technologies, then click Next to continue.
This chapter will explain some basic political system concepts in Victoria. Please click the politics button at the top.

Here shows Belgium's ruling party, the "Conservative Party." The policies they advocate have a significant impact on the nation and determine what policies the player can adopt. Below the party name you can see current policies. For example, the Nationalists favor state capitalism, one effect of which is that players can manually build factories, while under other policies only capitalists in the population can build factories. Another important influence of policies is that they restrict the freedom of the finance sliders. For example, a state capitalist party will not allow taxes to be below a certain level. Click Next to continue.

When the player encounters a ruling party they don't like, the system of government may greatly limit their ability to change it. The system of government can also prohibit certain ideological parties from taking power. Belgium's system of government is parliamentary constitutional monarchy, under which the government holds elections, but the player can choose to overturn election results and let another faction take power, despite increasing militancy among party supporters. The system of government is determined by various political reforms, and the player can only change it indirectly. For example, a democratic government cannot continue to exist when voting rights are abolished. Click Next to continue.

Some political systems generate ruling parties through elections, such as parliamentary constitutional monarchy and democratic republic. Elections for democratic governments must be held periodically, but the player can click the early election button to advance the election. After the election begins, the campaign follows. Various events often occur during campaigns, such as scandals and inflammatory speeches, enough to sway election results. After the campaign ends, voters decide the ruling party based on the policies they support. It's worth noting that voters and the entire population may not be equal — for example, in Belgium only the wealthy can vote. Click Next to continue.

Political reforms affect how the nation's political system operates and how the people view politics. For example, voting rights and electoral systems determine who can vote and who carries more weight in the vote. Media rights affect the political views of the educated population. The reason for political reforms is usually a call from the people, but may also be the player's desire to decide the nation's future more freely. Now let's look at social reforms, click Next to continue.

Social reforms affect the well-being of the nation. Some reforms increase industrial efficiency, such as maximum working hours. Others redistribute government funds to specific classes of people. Some social reforms are very beneficial to the nation, but note that social reforms increase administrative expenditure.

In the lower right of the politics panel you can see political decisions. These decisions have important effects on the nation, such as changing academic traditions, building the Panama Canal, and unifying Germany. Hover over the question mark to see prerequisites for executing decisions, and hover over the checkmark button to see their effects. If the checkmark button is gray, the player cannot execute these decisions because prerequisites are not met. Click Next to continue.

Finally let's look at the ultimate consequence of ignoring the people's suffering: revolution. As the militancy of the people increases, they will begin to join rebel factions, and these will be displayed in this window. Rebel factions are formed by a group of like-minded people dissatisfied with the status quo. We can see Belgium has a reactionist faction. To the right of its name there are three values:
Member Count - The number of people supporting the faction.
Organization - Represents the internal strength of the faction. This value increases when dissatisfied populations gain large incomes.
Rebellion Risk - Represents the risk of this faction staging an uprising.

When a rebel faction decides to rise up, a certain number of rebels will appear, determined by organization and rebellion risk. Be careful — if a pop's militancy is too high, it will rise up on its own regardless of the faction situation, and increase the overall uprising probability. You must defeat them in battle or address the demands of high-militancy pops to eliminate rebel factions. Click the Population tab to view the demands of each pop.
In this chapter, we will introduce more concepts about pops. Please click the population button at the top to continue the tutorial.

In Victoria II, the most basic unit of population is the pop. A pop represents a certain number of people within the same province, with the same occupation, ethnicity, and religion. Each pop has several characteristics, and we will help you familiarize yourself with them. Please click any pop icon to continue the tutorial.
Here we can further understand these "representatives of the people." First let's look at their attributes:
Nationality - Shows the language and ethnicity of this pop. Some nations are intolerant of ethnic minorities, which can cause friction.
Militancy - Shows the degree of dissatisfaction of this pop.
Consciousness - Shows this pop's understanding of the world around them and how to fight for their own rights.
Literacy Rate - Shows the literacy rate of this pop. This affects research points, the efficiency of the pop as various professionals, and the pop's political orientation.
Religion - Shows this pop's beliefs. If different from the state religion, it can cause friction.
Unemployment Rate - Shows what proportion of people in this pop are unemployed.

Need Satisfaction - Shows how much of this pop's material needs are met. Unmet needs can lead to various outcomes: unmet luxury needs may make the pop unhappy, while unmet basic needs mean starvation.
Please close the window to continue.
Let's further explore the two most important indices: militancy and consciousness

Consciousness - The greatest role of consciousness in the game is driving reforms. As the game progresses and the nation develops, consciousness will continue to grow, and the people will begin to demand reforms. If pops obtain the reforms they expect, consciousness will decrease somewhat. Another important effect of increased consciousness is that pops will begin to have greater demands, making it possible for wealthy autocratic governments to avoid reforms by making the people richer.

Militancy - Many things can make pops angry, but the most important one is the people's inability to meet basic survival needs. Pop anger is accompanied by a higher probability of riots. When a pop is extremely angry, it will join a revolutionary party and use all its resources to overthrow the government, even rising up as rebels.

Finally, you will notice that pops have cash. Pops earn cash from their occupation. This money is used to purchase life necessities. If a pop has surplus money, it may deposit it in the national bank, allowing the nation to borrow from the national bank.
In this chapter, we will introduce the concept of trade in Victoria II. Please click the trade button at the top to enter the trade interface.

In Victoria II, all products flow through the global market. Every day, all pops, factories, and governments try to purchase life necessities, raw materials, and various resources from the market. Click Next to continue the tutorial.

Prices are determined daily by the market based on global supply and demand. Imbalances in supply and demand create an ideal price, and the current price will gradually move toward it. Pay attention to the prices of goods important to the player. For example, if the price of light weapons is rising, it may be time to build new factories. Click Continue

Some trade can be automatic, such as materials for maintaining the army, navy, and overseas assets, and raw materials needed for construction. Note the auto-trade checkbox is ticked, meaning trade is automatic. Let's try manual trading — click the checkbox to untick it.

Manual trade can be used to stockpile inventory and set daily purchase quantities for certain goods. Move the slider to the desired position — this means if your stockpile will be maintained at this level, excess goods will be sold. Click the confirm trade button.

The market is divided into two parts: the domestic market and the global market. The common market refers to the domestic market plus the markets of other nations within the same sphere of influence. The world market includes all goods outside the common market. When buyers prepare to purchase goods, they first try to buy from the common market. When common market stock cannot meet their demand, they will import from the world market. The correct way to build a domestic economy is to ensure the goods your nation needs are all produced domestically. Click Next to continue.
In this chapter, we will further introduce rankings and the diplomacy interface. Please click the diplomacy button at the top.
In Victoria II, rankings are very important. A higher ranking brings advantages and respect. Rankings are composed of three indices:

Prestige - Prestige increases from improving the nation's condition, such as winning wars, building colonies, or developing culture. Prestige is an extremely important value, because nations with high prestige have priority in purchasing on the global market. The highest-prestige nation has the right to purchase any goods first.
Industry - Industry score increases from strengthening industrial power, i.e., building factories and railways.
Military - Military score is based on army strength. Large warships provide the highest score bonus. Note that as new ship types emerge, old ships eliminated by the times become worthless.
These parameters together determine a nation's ranking. Click the # in the nation list to get ranking information.
Currently the most important nation is Britain. Our Belgium still needs to work hard in the rankings.
Nation Name and Flag - The nation's name and the flag that symbolizes it.
Influence Priority - Here you can choose which nation to prioritize influence on. Only Great Powers can do this to non-Great Powers. Unfortunately our nation's strength is insufficient.
Great Power Influence - Here you can view the degree of influence each of the eight Great Powers has on the world.
Sphere of Influence - Here you can check whether a nation is within another nation's sphere of influence.
Scores - In order: nation's prestige ranking, industry ranking, military ranking, and total ranking.

Opinion - All non-Great Power nations have their own opinion of Great Power nations. From "hostile" to "within sphere of influence," these opinions determine how welcome a nation is to the Great Power. If a nation holds a friendly attitude toward a Great Power and the Great Power has sufficient influence, it can choose to place that nation in its sphere of influence.
Relations - Your relations with this nation. You can choose to increase this value to make the nation friendlier, but after many years, this value will return to zero.
Please click Luxembourg, which is in the sphere of influence of the Netherlands.
Here you can see the national information of Luxembourg.
You can see the nation is an absolutist civilized nation, ruled by conservatives.
Here you can find rankings and scores.
Here you can see how much influence Great Powers have on Luxembourg. When the player becomes a Great Power, this information becomes very important.
Please find Britain in the list and click it.

As you can see, Britain is a Great Power (actually the strongest). Its info is similar, but without Great Power influence and with sphere of influence added. After the player becomes a Great Power, pay attention to what nations your competitors want to control. Click Next to continue.
In this chapter, we will discuss some more advanced concepts in Victoria II, including concepts that first-generation players may not have encountered. Select your Belgian army to begin the tutorial.

In Victoria II, every army you build requires a pop (representing a portion of your population) as a recruitment source. Note the soldier icon next to all brigades in your army — this icon indicates the unit is connected to a soldier pop. Most of your units are connected to soldiers, except for those mobilized during total war.

This connection is very realistic in Victoria II. Losses to the army are reflected in the connected pop. If a pop riots, the corresponding army will mutiny together. You should remember this well, especially when you mobilize a large number of your population and send them to die in the trenches. Click Next to continue.

Your units also need supplies to fight — the army needs light weapons and canned food, and the navy needs sailing ships. These supplies must be purchased by your government from the market, and the purchase process can be automatic (default) or manual in the trade interface. Hover over the supply bar to see this army's needs and whether they are met. Click Next to continue.

We said before that if a pop connected to an army mutinies, the corresponding unit will also rebel. You can see one of our units has a rebel faction icon, which means its corresponding pop belongs to a faction. This is very dangerous. One way to check this pop's status and issues is to click this population icon, which will open the corresponding population interface. Click Next to continue.
Now let's discuss some more advanced concepts about goods output and profit distribution. Let's first click the production button at the top.

In Victoria II, factories are not the only place where we can produce goods. In this "production interface," you can see all goods being produced. Note that some goods have an artisan icon next to them, indicating they are produced by artisans.

Artisans don't work in factories or RGOs. They buy the materials they need from the market, process these raw materials into new goods, and then sell them. The proceeds from the sale are used to purchase the artisan's daily necessities. Artisans are the main producers of secondary processed goods in the early game, but as the game progresses, they are squeezed out by factories benefiting from new technologies. Now let's discuss profit distribution. Click Next.

Like artisans, factories and RGOs also need to sell their products on the market to earn money to maintain operations. Sales revenue minus raw material expenditure (RGOs have no expenditure) is their profit, which is then distributed to these pops:

Owners - Nobles are the owners of RGOs, and capitalists are the owners of factories. They bring production bonuses, and in return they receive a large portion of the profit, which is then divided equally among all owners in the region.

Workers - RGOs correspond to farmers and laborers, factories to craftsmen and clerks. Workers receive the remaining profit of the corresponding factory or RGO (minimum wage affects this), and use their income to purchase their needs.
Sometimes factories need a little help from the player. Click Next to find out what.

Sometimes you may want a loss-making factory to continue operating — you may need to continue producing important strategic resources, or simply want to keep workers happy. The money to ensure the factory doesn't lose money comes from your treasury. Select the factory subsidy checkbox to start subsidizing your steel mill.
Now let's discuss some more advanced concepts about finance, such as gold and government employees. Let's open the finance interface.

Most of the expenditure slider is used to pay salaries of your government employees, and these expenditures are divided equally among the same type of pops. Regardless of how much you pay them, these pops will complete their tasks equally. However, if you don't pay enough, these people will start changing jobs or even rebel. Conversely, if you pay them a lot, more people will switch to these occupations. This means if you need more of a certain type of person, such as soldiers or bureaucrats, you can increase their funds. But be careful not to let them expand too much. Let's go through these government employees. Click Next to continue.
Our education expenditure pays the clergy who represent educators. They not only teach your people to read and write, but also teach them political beliefs.
Lower Consciousness - The growth of consciousness of pops in provinces with clergy is reduced, and this effect is more pronounced on the poor class.
Increase Literacy Rate - Literacy rate in provinces with clergy increases. When clergy make up 4% of the population, additional clergy will no longer increase this effect.
Click Next to enter the administrative section.
Our administrative expenditure pays our bureaucrats, who ensure the normal operation of the modern state. They have the following effects:

Administrative Efficiency - Your nation's administrative efficiency affects your tariff efficiency and the effectiveness of social reforms. Administrative efficiency is determined by your technology and the ratio of bureaucrats to total population. The proportion of bureaucrats needed for maximum efficiency increases with social reforms. More social reforms require more bureaucrats. To find out how many bureaucrats you need, hover over the bureaucrat proportion.

To make the best use of your bureaucrats, you should keep them at an optimal ratio. How you control this depends on how you manage administrative expenditure and whether your other pops are satisfied with their work. Click Next to continue.

Social expenditure funds your social reforms. This money is not paid directly to any government employee, but to the government agency corresponding to the reform. Unemployment benefits are paid to unemployed pops, while pensions are divided equally among all pops. You can see Belgium's expenditure is 0, because we have no social reforms. Now let's end the expenditure discussion and begin discussing gold. Click Next.

Rare metals are a special type of goods — they are not sold on the world market, but are directly converted to money and distributed to mine employees and the nation controlling the mine. Note this is the only place in Victoria II's economic system that directly generates money, and if world productivity doesn't increase, this will cause inflation. Now let's learn more about loans. Click Next to continue.

As mentioned earlier in this tutorial, a nation can always take loans from the world bank. Since we've said gold is the only way money enters the economic system, we should examine where the money you borrow comes from.

Pops deposit part of their earnings in the national bank. When a nation needs to borrow, this money comes from various national banks — first from the nation's own bank, then from other nations' banks based on their size. If you don't have a loan yet, take one now, then click Next.

In the "Borrow" list you can see a series of nations — these are your creditor nations. When you pay interest or repay loans, this money returns to the lending pops in the order of the creditor nations' fleet counts.

When you cannot pay interest, you are considered to be in default. In this case, your creditor nations can use their navies to force you to enact certain economic policies to repay your debts. Defaulting is very bad, and you should avoid this situation as much as possible. Click Next to continue.
In this section we will introduce several important political concepts in Victoria II. Let's open the politics interface.

First is pluralism. It reflects the population within your nation that expects reforms. A higher value means louder calls for reform. Its positive meaning is that it can bring more progressives and generate more research points. Pluralism increases over time, and it also increases certain technological progress. When you hover over pluralism, you can view Belgium's current pluralism.

Revanchism represents the anger your people feel about the injustice your nation has suffered in international society. When our nation loses a core territory, revanchism increases until we recapture it or let time fade it away. When revanchism reaches a certain level, your people will tend more toward chauvinism and fascism.

The upper house is key to formulating reform proposals. When certain parties control the upper house, you may be unable to implement certain social and political reforms. This is because different parties have different attitudes toward reforms. For example, when fascist parties are in opposition, they don't support any reforms, until conservative parties are forced to reform due to high domestic militancy.
On the left you can see which reforms and ideas Belgium's upper house currently supports.
The composition of upper house parties depends on upper house policy reforms. Hover over different options to view different parties' opinions on reforms. Click Next to continue.

We implement social reforms to make our people's lives better. But there is a cost issue. Most reforms increase expenditure and the scale of your bureaucracy. However, there are two exceptions: unemployment subsidies and pensions are paid directly to the people to support their basic needs. Pensions are paid to all citizens, with the nation supporting 20% of each pop's basic needs. Unemployment subsidies are paid to unemployed pops. Click Next to continue the tutorial.
Here we will discuss population movements, ideology, and political views. Let's open the population interface first.
Your people hold various ideologies and political views, which change over time. We can divide the factors that cause changes into two categories:
Current Status — The current employment situation of the pop. If the pop is unemployed, it will support unemployment subsidy reforms.
Pop Type — Different pops, even under the same conditions, tend to develop in different ideological directions. Soldiers tend toward militarism, while capitalists tend toward liberalism.

These factors interact, increasing or decreasing pop demands over time. Pop ideologies oscillate left and right under their influence. You can satisfy their demands to appease them or build a loyal army. Hover over the proportion chart to see why they support these ideas.
Let's learn about promotion and demotion. Select a pop from the list.
In Victoria II, you don't need to manually manage employment of each pop. They will automatically choose corresponding occupations based on their current status.

Promotion and Demotion — If a pop's current status is good, they will gradually try to find higher-level positions than their current occupation. If things are bad, they will move to lower-level positions. Hover over these values to see which factors affect them.
New Positions — You can see what positions these pops are considering or aspiring to. Hover over them for more details.

These changes are "gradual." If you expect a certain industry to develop faster, you need to increase the attractiveness of that industry to make your people more willing to leave their current class and change occupations. Check which factors affect their decisions, then strengthen or weaken them.
Migration in Victoria II follows a relatively simple pattern: it proceeds slowly according to the current state of pops. There are three types of migration driving your people:
Domestic Migration — Pops migrate domestically, moving to areas with easy employment.
Foreign Migration — Pops migrate to other nations, such as nations with more lenient religious policies.
Colonial Migration — Pops move in or out of your colonies to seek a fresh start.
These changes are very slow. If you want to know their migration motives, you can check the information in this interface.
We will briefly mention some concepts new to original Victoria I players and summarize the government's role in trade. Let's open the trade interface.
In Victoria II, all entities like factories and artisans participate in trade on their own, which limits the government's responsibilities to:

Supplying Overseas Provinces — To effectively use overseas provinces you need to supply them with convoys. Every province not connected to your capital by land increases demand for convoys. If you don't meet this demand, the production efficiency of those provinces' factories and RGOs will be penalized.
Supplying Your Troops — Your troops need goods like canned food and weapons. If they don't get enough, their efficiency will be penalized.

Construction — Building units or factories requires consuming goods. When you build, the needed goods are prioritized from stockpile. If some goods are insufficient, they will be added to your government demand. When capitalists build factories, they purchase the needed goods themselves
column3: you only need to supply the goods for manually constructed buildings.

column2: Stockpile — The government stockpiles goods for the people to use. The necessity of this is to maintain various goods supplies during trade blockades. When you select the "Buy from Stockpile" checkbox, your people will also purchase goods from the stockpile in addition to buying from the market. This avoids the high costs during blockades.

When your trade is automatic, your government orders will strictly match its needs. When you form a new unit, trade orders will be set to meet the increased demand. However, sometimes we need to save money. For this purpose you can click a certain good in government demand and cancel its automatic trade setting. This way you can freely set any trade you want.
Let's summarize how trade and the market work. All goods produced in Victoria II are supplied to the market for sale.

Common Market — The first round of trade occurs in the common market, which is the market between a nation and its sphere of influence members. All buyers in the market first try to purchase goods from here.

Export to Global Market — Goods not sold in the common market are exported to the global market. In this market, nations and their citizens purchase in order of prestige, so if a good is very scarce, the role of prestige becomes very important. Goods not sold in the global market will be wasted, and producers only get paid if they sell their goods.

In conclusion, if you try to ensure stable goods supplies for the nation and get your people paid, two things are very important: having high prestige to ensure your people get a front position in the queue, and ensuring sufficient stock in your common market to maintain your economy.
In this chapter we will focus on war and peace, and Great Power diplomacy. This time, let's switch to the Great Power, Prussia. Now enter the diplomacy interface.
The eight nations in the upper left are Great Powers, as you can see we are also one of them.

Being a Great Power has many benefits, such as having your own sphere of influence, ethnic minorities in the nation being happier, and being able to colonize. Losing Great Power status will also make your people very uneasy.
Beyond Great Powers there are several other tiers. Secondary Powers can also colonize. Uncivilized nations cannot industrialize until they become civilized.
Want to know how to become a Great Power? Click Continue to find out.
How to Become (or be Kicked Out of) Great Power
Whether you can become a Great Power depends on your scores, including prestige, military, and industry points. Our current scores keep us firmly seated in the Great Power position.

If you're about to fall out of the Great Power seat, it's not too late to remedy — you have a period to solve this problem. One way is to start a war, which can increase your prestige or lower others' prestige. Now find France and declare war on her.
In this generation of the game, you must have a war goal when declaring war. Now goals are listed in the war declaration menu. Choose one you like and click OK.

Your goals can be more than just those at declaration. If your people support militarism and you have enough war score, you can add war goals in this interface. But if you can't complete these goals, your people will be very angry. Now click the table showing Great Powers.

Sphere of Influence means a nation is under the influence of a more powerful nation. The biggest benefit is that you will have a common market and keep your economy prosperous. Another important point is that if you want to unify the nation, you must bring all powers occupying your nation's core provinces into your sphere of influence. Want to know how to get a sphere of influence? Click Continue.
To get a sphere of influence, two things are important: influence and opinion between the two nations.

Influence on a nation increases over time (of course you must set a priority first). Our goal is to unify Germany, but Hanover holds the German core. Find Hanover in the nation list and increase your priority to it to the maximum.

Currently Hanover's opinion of us is "Neutral." (Note this is not the numerically displayed relations!) To pull it into the sphere of influence, the opinion must be raised to "Friendly." Now there is an action in diplomacy to improve opinion. If you hover over it, you can see our influence is insufficient. Now that the priority is set to the highest, just wait.

If other nations also try to influence Hanover, we can counterattack. For example, expelling advisors can damage other nations' relations with Hanover. That requires relations above "Neutral." Don't worry, no one will disturb us now.
As the game progresses, the diplomatic war intensifies, and we can also directly use force to seize others' spheres of influence. Click Continue.
This chapter will provide more explanation of various technology categories and institutions. Open the research interface.

At the top are shown various research institutions, indicating our nation's strengths and weaknesses in various areas. As you can see, Prussia is a military-industrial complex with great advantages in army research but disadvantages in culture. You can change the research institution in decisions. If your military expenditure remains high, your people will be more willing to join the military. Now let's talk about industrial technology, click the industrial technology interface.

Industrial technology relates to your road to industrialization, including research on railways, factories, and mining. Note that some industrial technologies bring simultaneous benefits to all areas. Now switch to cultural technology.

Cultural technology includes various literature and psychology, national focus, and education. Many cultural technologies bring you prestige — the earlier you research them, the more prestige you gain. Now switch to the commercial technology interface.

Commercial technology includes banking, economic theory, and monetary systems, which are very helpful for increasing tax revenue and administrative efficiency, though they require a corresponding industrial base. Now please switch to the naval technology interface.
These technologies are self-explanatory — they allow you to build larger, faster ships and increase supply range to colonize more distant regions.

Many army technologies provide bonuses to all your units, such as supply efficiency, attack power, and organization. In the bottom technologies, you can build some new units such as tanks and aircraft. Click Next to continue.
Welcome to the World of Victoria II

This is an introduction to Victoria II, set in the 19th century. This is an era when new worlds are born, old worlds fade, and new technologies, ideas, and revolutionaries emerge like mushrooms after rain. Where shall we begin? Click Continue.
In the game you must select a nation. For the tutorial we'll use Belgium, a nation that's not difficult for beginners but has great potential for development.
In the upper left corner you can see your flag, scores, and ranking. Click Continue.

There are many ways to change your nation's fate in the game. There are many indirect methods like changing laws and increasing taxes. At the top there are eight important interfaces to guide your nation, where you can also get much information. The meanings of these eight interfaces are as follows:
Production — You can view industry and production situations.
Finance — Money is important in the game. In the finance interface you can control national taxes and expenditure.
Research — You can research new technologies here, each of which can enhance your nation's power.
Politics — An important part of Victoria. Different political systems and parties can carry out various reforms, and the interests of different groups vary.
Population — Your population includes various pops living within the nation, and is also an important part of the game. Your various actions will affect your people.

Trade — Various industrial and agricultural products must be traded for money. You cannot interfere with others' trade, but you need to purchase necessary goods for your government, and can monitor the entire market in this interface.
Diplomacy — Another major part of the game. Various actions from allying to controlling other nations will bring various influences on your position in the world.
Military — Finally, the military interface. Any political and diplomatic action requires strong military force as backing.
